utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: My name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues Mr. Williamson, Mr. Waespi and Mr. Vos for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am Tomas Fila. I am here with Mr. Petrovic and together we are here for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Can you hear me, Mr. Dokmanovic? I would like to thank Mr. Fila for providing the Prosecutor and the court with the written text of his opening statement. This will enable you to focus on the main points, if you see what I mean. Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are a couple of other matters if we can attend to them before we get to Mr. Fila's statement. The documents that I was speaking of yesterday which we were expecting to receive from the UN in New York, we have, in fact, received in part. We still have not, as of yet, received the ultimatum from General Kadijevic to the Croat Government, but we did receive the listing from the Secretary-General of the notification of sucession by the Government of Croatia to 29 treaties effective as of 8 October 1991 and, additionally, the final report of the Badinter Commission on the issue of effective dates of independence. This is opinion number 11 from July of 1993 in which they fix the effective date of independence of Croatia and Slovenia as 8 October 1991. At this time, I would like to tender this. I believe this will be Prosecutor's exhibit 192.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: A copy has already been provided to the Defence. Additionally, in response to Mr. Fila's request yesterday for this videotape, we have gone through the videotape in its entirety. The only portion that we can find that we think possibly is what he is talking about -- it is not from French television; it is from Serb television -- it is in 1994 and not 1990 and it refers to Mr. Dokmanovic not as the "former mayor" of Vukovar, but as the "new mayor" of Vukovar. If that is what he is requesting, we can show it, but that is the closest we can come to what he is talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, my associate will be coming here today and bringing experts from Belgrade. He will also bring that tape that I received from you, so I will show it to you tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, you may now make your opening statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I shall present it more briefly than as I have written it. As you know, it is also a response to two Prosecutor briefs so I am really dealing with three matters all together. The opening of the Defence: The creation and break-up of the Yugoslavia State. The creation of the first Yugoslavia -- the Yugoslav state was created after the First World War in 1918 by the unification of two then independent States -- the Kingdom of Serbia and the Kingdom of Montenegro and of territories of the former Austro-Hungarian monarchy inhabited by South Slav peoples, Serbs, Croats and Slovenes. Pursuant to the decision of the National Council of the State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs, those territories were annexed to the new Yugoslav State which was initially called the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes and later the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. This was a unitary State based on the State thesis of one people with three entities -- Serbs, Croats and Slovenes. It was divided into banovinas. They were a territorial division along administrative rather than ethnic lines. The declaration of Nis of 1914, in which the Government and National Assembly of the Kingdom of Serbia opted for a joint State of the Yugoslav peoples, shows that the Serbs had already made such a decision during the First World War. It is important to mention that they consciously sacrificed their national and State identity created during the 19th century and accepted the idea of a trinomial named South Slav people. In that State, the Serbs felt nationally united, all of them living in the same State. The Prosecution's thesis and that of its experts of the Yugoslav State as the realisation of the idea of a "Greater Serbia", has no grounds because the first Yugoslav state brought national and state emancipation to the Croat and Slovene peoples for the first time in their history. The Allied powers in 1915, in London, offered by the Treaty of London, the creation of a Greater Serbia, the Serb Government rejected that offer, opting instead for unification with other Slav peoples. It was then that the term "Greater Serbia" appeared for the first and only time in international law. From the very inception of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, there were many strong antagonisms. This was the consequence of the different and mutually exclusive State and national programmes of the Yugoslav peoples. This intolerance and latent separatism were manifested through the Croat parliamentary boycott and heavy propaganda against the creation of a joint State built on democratic principles. The Croats and Slovenes, in my opinion, consciously abused the Yugoslav idea. After the First World War, the Slovenes left the circle of the defeated to enter the circle of the victors. The Croats did the same after the Second World War. By joining the circle of the winning powers, they avoided responsibilities and obligations to pay war reparations. Therefore, the representative of Italy at the 1919 Conference of Versailles, for almost a year would not consent to letting the Delineation Commission start work. He refused to sit at the same table with the representatives of the defeated powers because a representative of the Croats, Dr. Trumbic, was on the delegation of the new state of Yugoslavia. The Croat and Slovene political elite saw the Yugoslav State as a transitional period in the process of gaining State and national independence. For example, the prominent Slovene politician Anton Korosec, who was a Minister in all the governments of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia from 1918 to 1941, explained the reasons why the Slovenes joined Yugoslavia. He said: "We have mounted a good horse. We will return a worn out nag." However, for the Serbs, the creation of this kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes according to how King Alexander envisaged the creation of the Yugoslav nation that would be developed "through barracks and schools", represented for the Serbs the fulfilment of their centuries-long dream of the free and joint life of a single Yugoslav nation in a single Yugoslav state. The Break up of the first Yugoslavia. The German invasion in 1941 spelled the end of the first Yugoslavia and the beginning of the Golgotha of the Serb nation in the independent State of Croatia, formed in the meantime by the Ustashas under German patronage. Already in the 1930s an Ustasha terrorist organisation was established, the ultimate objective of which was the creation of an independent State of Croatia and the extermination of the Serb population. The establishment of Ustasha rule saw an unprecedented persecution of the Serb population which became genocide on the most massive scale. The Serbs were compelled to defend themselves; they rose up and organised resistance to German and Ustasha terror. The creation of the second Yugoslavia. Upon the victory of the Allies in the Second World War, the Yugoslav State was created on a Federal basis with six republics -- Serbia, Croatia, Slovenia, Macedonia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Montenegro. As distinct from the other four republics, the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina were proclaimed republics with a number of constituent peoples; the Republic of Croatia as the State of the Croat and Serb peoples, and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as the State of Serb Muslim and Croat peoples. The communist rule established in 1945 strongly suppressed national hatreds, myths and stereotypes. The Ustasha crime went unpunished. The victims and the executioners were reconciled in brotherhood and unity, the universal formula for resolving the national question in socialist Yugoslavia. There was no catharsis of the Croat people; no Croat Willy Brandt emerged to apologise to the Serb and other victims of Ustasha madness in Jasenovac and other camps. The evil was shut away in Pandora's box. Ignoring political and ethnic realities, the leadership of the Communist Party of Yugoslavia arbitrarily drew administrative borders between the republics, which several decades later are to become State borders and along with the unresolved national question, they became the second major cause of the civil war. Josip Broz Tito, an ethnic Croat was the unassailable ruler of Yugoslavia for decades. Still, even at the time of his rule, Croat separatism resurged in the form of the Maspok, spreading ideas about redesigning of Yugoslavia, the covert objective being its dismemberment and the creation of an independent Croat state. During this period, the persecution of Serbs started again in the form of dismissal from work in sweeping numbers. Tito settled scores with the advocates of the Maspok by arresting them, among them Tudjman and Mesic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Could you please slow down a little bit for the interpreters? Slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: They have a text. I am sorry, I thought that they had a translation of the text, too, because I gave it to them earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: If you slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Tito settled scores with the advocates of the Maspok by arresting them, among them Tudjman and Mesic. Yugoslavia remained intact for the time being but the idea lived on. The Break-up of the Second Yugoslavia. Clericalism and the Ustasha movement returned to the political scene of Croatia in 1990, seeing the Serbs in Croatia as their enemy and proclaiming them as in the days of Ante Starcevic, a "disruptive factor". The finale of that process was the assumption of power by the Croat Democratic Union, the HDZ. By the 1990 amendments to the Constitution of the Republic of Croatia, that is the one that the Prosecutor presented as evidence, from a constituent nation, that is to say, one of the two equal constituent peoples of Croatia, they were turned into a national minority. Serbs were again being fired from State and local bodies of authority, from the judiciary, educational establishments, hospitals and factories. Croatia's separatism culminated in secession, in contravention of the provisions of the constitution of the SFRY which required the consent of all the federal units for any change in the State borders. Not only was the SFRY constitution violated, but so was the constitution of the Republic of Croatia because a decision on legal secession was impossible to take without the consent of one of the two constituent peoples in that republic, that is to say the Serb people. Parallel with the Croat referendum on independence and sovereignty, the Serbs in Croatia, as they felt imperilled, organised a referendum of their own at which they opted to stay in Yugoslavia. Illegal secession compounded by physical pressures, dismissals from work and evictions, physical assaults, threats and insults, instilled the feeling in the Serbs they were only a step away from a second pogrom in 50 years. In such a situation, the Serbs in Croatia had no option but to organise their self-defence in areas in which they were in the majority and to look to the Federal State as their state for protection. The Federal State, where the President of the presidency was Stipe Mesic, a Croat; the Federal Prime Minister, was Ante Markovic, a Croat; and the Defence Minister was Veljko Kadijevic, a Croat; the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Loncar, a Croat -- did not accept secession and such behaviour on the part of Croatia (nor on the part of Slovenia for that matter) and the JNA as the armed force of the SFRJ intervened. The objective was preservation of the SFRY which had a constitutional obligation and separation of the rebel Croats and the Serbs were defending themselves from the former. The claim made under count 4 of the indictment that the JNA intervened in support of the Serb insurgents is incorrect, just as it is an arbitrary statement to say in Count 11 of the indictment that the Serb authorities listed identifying information about the people imprisoned in Ovcara, for no Serb authorities existed there. It was either the JNA or paramilitary troops in the territory of Ovcara. It should be reiterated here that, apart from its illegal secession in terms of the SFRY constitution, the Republic of Croatia did not fulfil any of the three constitutive requirements according to the rules of international law and the practice of states for an entity so aspiring to be considered a State, it would have to have a given territory, to have a given population and to wield sovereign authority in that territory. Not a single one of these things was true in the Republic of Croatia. The declaration of European Community Foreign Ministers of 17 December 1991, the communiqué of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the kingdom of The Netherlands of 24 December says, "The presidency of the European Community invites the six republics in Yugoslavia to state whether they wish to be recognised as independent States and to accept the commitments contained in the letter of 17 December 1991; positive replies have been received from Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia, Macedonia and Slovenia. The Presidency has informed the Chair of the Conference on Yugoslavia accordingly, asking that these applications be referred to the Arbitration Commission to render its opinion." I wish to note once again that this is all happening after the period that is relevant to the indictment, because this is 17 December 1991. That was the end of the second Yugoslavia and the second attempt to put into practice the idea of a joint Yugoslavia State of the South Slavs and I hope that this is the last such attempt. My hope stems from tragic experience. All attempts at creating Yugoslavia in the 20th century have cost dearly -- several million victims and untold numbers of people driven away from their homes. B. The Serbs in Croatia. Historical facts. Historical material indicates that the Serbs have been present in the territory of what is today the Republic of Croatia since the 14th century. The ethnic space of the Serbs stretched from Northern Dalmatia via Lika, Kordun, Gorski Kotar, to the border from the Slovene lands. Banija, the area around Pakrac and Daruvar to Eastern Slavonia, the areas of the cities of Osijek and Vukovar. Most of the Serbs inhabiting at that time had the status of imperial frontier guards men, while the others were dependent peasants - serfs. In the cities and pre-towns there were Serb tradesmen. The Croato-Hungarian agreement gave birth to the Greater Croat ideology, whose theses on the Croats "historical rights" negated the Serbs as a nation, denying their national distinctiveness and equality in Croat lands. The Croat Party of Rights headed by Ante Starcevic defined the Serb people as "Croats of the Eastern faith", calling the Serbs non brethren, Byzantines, and a "disruptive factor". Croat chauvinism culminated in the emergence of the Ustasha movement in the 1930s. The Ustasha saw a solution to the Croat national and state question in the physical elimination of the Serb people living in the territories to the west of the Drina river. In 1941, with the occupation of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, clerical fascists, headed by Ante Pavelic, assumed power in Croatia. Hitler made it possible for the independent State of Croatia to encompass the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the whole of Srem. The Ustasha leader, with the leader, Ante Pavelic, embarked on an unprecedented and unparalleled persecution of the Serbs. The political and state platform of the Independent State of Croatia was defined by a single slogan: a third of the Serbs to be converted, a third displaced and a third killed. Tens of thousands of Serbs, perhaps hundreds of thousands, ended their lives in Ustasha death camps in Jasenovac, Jadovno and Stara Gradiska. About 200,000 Serbs were deported to Serbia. Race laws were enacted against Serbs, Jews and the Romanies. Orthodox Serbs were converted en masse to Catholicism with the support of the Catholic church. May I show you a segment from the videotape about killing and converting to Catholicism?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This is the Jasenovac concentration camp. (Videotape played). "Public service of the Ustasha Defence, Jasenovac concentration camp 1941 to 1945." (Videotape continues).

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Those are the Jews. These are the children that were killed in Jasenovac -- Serb children. These are Pavelic and Hitler that you saw a moment ago -- this is the environs of Jasenovac. That is a map of the concentration camp itself. This is what was called a Srbosek, a special device for killing Serbs. This is another device which they used to kill them. This is an Ustashe at work. These are the Ustasha caps which were forcibly put on the heads of Serb children -- they were made to wear them. This is the compulsory conversion of the Serbs en masse to Catholicism in the camp itself." (Videotape ended). The suffering of the Serbs from 1941 to 1945 in the Vukovar area, that is the subject of our discussions here. The genocidal policy of the Ustasha regime in its most horrendous form was carried out in the area of Velika Zupa which encompassed 10 districts, 7 towns and 156 municipalities. According to the 1931 census, 439,900 inhabitants lived in this area, 211,000 Serbs (48 per cent) and 118,000 Croats (27 per cent). The witch hunt against the Serb people of the Vuka Welika Zupanija started in mid April 1941. First the Ustasha authorities banned the use of the Cyrillic alphabet and took down all inscriptions in the Cyrillic script. This was followed by arrests carried out by municipal authorities. Individuals and so on. Eminent and well-to-do Serbs, volunteers from the First World War, members of the Soko Yugoslav sports association and of various Serb cultural and educational associations, were put in prison. Some of them were liquidated summarily, many vanished without a trace and others were deported to camps. A similar fate was to befall the Romanies and the Jews, 1,620 Romanies of whom 500 children and 500 Jews were deported to the camp of Jasenovac in 1941 and 1942 alone. The Ustasha "Court Martial" was constantly in session in Vukovar. There are documents attesting to its rulings -- 15 persons were shot dead on 31 July 1941, 20 inhabitants of Negoslavci, Brsadin and Borovo were shot dead on 17 January 1942, 57 inhabitants of Stara Pazova, Stari Banovci and other places were shot dead on 27 September 1941 and later in 1942. According to the report of the Commission for Establishing the Crimes of the Occupiers and Those Who Assisted Them, from Vukovar imprisoned the Serbs. One composition full of women and one containing 50 men arrived in Jasenovac. The following day, on 27 August 1942, another train consisting of 20 wagons full of Serbs was formed. Its journey to Jasenovac took two days and two nights. Upon its arrival at the camp, the women and children were separated and transferred across to the Sava River to Gradina. They were all immediately liquidated. 8,000 Serbs were converted to Catholicism in the area of Vukovar, 4,000 Serbs were killed during the period of the Ustasha genocide from 1941 to 1945 and many became displaced persons. The idea of genocide against the Serb people in the Vukovar area during World War II bore fruit. The ethnic composition in this area was changed completely. According to the 1991 population census, which has been tendered in evidence, this area was inhabited mainly by Croats 43.7 per cent, followed by Serbs 37.4 per cent and others 19 per cent. The position of Serbs in Croatia from 1945 to 1995 with special reference to Vukovar. With the creation of the communist Yugoslavia, the Serb people believed that their sufferings had come to an end. They believed in the strength of the Communist Party of Yugoslavia and its ideology of "brotherhood and unity", which rejected identification and punishment of the guilty. It reconciled them by force and equalised them in suffering and guilt. The Ustasha concentration camp of Jasenovac was razed to the ground by the communists. Traces of the crime were obliterated from the face of the earth but not from collective memory of the Serb people. The Serbs were asked to forgive and forget. Nothing was asked of the Croat people. They were not asked to name their criminals or to punish them. The Serbs exhibited goodwill. En mass they entered into mixed marriages, all for the sake of Yugoslavia and brotherhood with other nations and nationalities. They consciously renounced their own history, their national identity, and above all their Orthodox faith. The majority of those who declared themselves as Yugoslavs hailed from Serb milieus, primarily from the large towns in Serbia. They were therefore all the more surprised at the resurgence of the Ustasha movement. The Maspok, the mass movement in 1968 rallied around the Matica Hrvatska Society, gave rise to a new euphoria in Croatia and with it came the persecution of the Serbs. Tito stopped this wave but only temporarily. Again, not all the culprits were named, many got away. The year 1990 saw a new tragedy for the Serbs in the Vukovar area. The Croat Democratic Union,, the HDZ, won a convincing victory at the elections for the Croat Assembly. However, on the territory of the Vukovar municipality, they did not win a majority. The Party of democratic change won the majority of seats in the Municipal Assembly. They were former communists and with them, Councillor Slavko Dokmanovic was elected. However, a changed political climate could be felt in the city already at that time -- a political climate. Activities were conducted aimed at intimidating inhabitants of Serb nationality. The results of this was their exodus from their homesteads. Serbs were illegally arrested and searched in an organised fashion. They were ousted from leadership positions and threatened with physical liquidation. At the same time, the Croats were procuring arms, forming armed groups and blowing up buildings belonging to the Serbs -- business outlets, shops, et cetera. The public services, courts, educational institutions and the hospital were purged of Serb personnel. Dr. Rade Popovic, who was the head of the Vukovar hospital, was replaced with Dr. Vesna Bosanac. Members of the HDZ took Radio Vukovar by force and appointed a new director, a Croat, a member of the HDZ. The makeup of the police station also changed. People loyal to the HDZ assumed responsible positions in order to protect the points via which the Croats were pulling in weapons and military equipment to Vukovar. One of the first victims was Zeliko Ostojic. In 1990 he testified before JNA security bodies about the existence of these groups, about the intentions and plans of Glavas, Mercep and Zadro to ethnically cleanse Eastern Slavonia. In the night between 25 and 26 January 1991, Ostojic was killed in his flat in Borovo Naselje. His killing coincided with the showing of the film about General Martin Spegelj. He was a general of the JNA, who brokered the illicit importation and distribution of weapons in Croatia and was aired on TV that same evening. May we have an excerpt from that film? . (Videotape played). "This is if you need it at the decisive moment. This is Croatia's Defence Minister and the second is the Minister of Police. Organise two or three men for the liquidation of the most dangerous. The physical liquidation dum, dum, dum -- our police does not dare. Yes, it does, we go to one and then another at the same time. Those who are the most dangerous can be killed at their door steps. No questions are asked, do not ask whether there are women, children, nothing, no questions asked. As far as watch towers are concerned, when there is the disarmament of the watch towers, everybody will be disarmed, as many people as exist, but leave the Albanians five bullets a piece in their automatic rifles and, the others, you should keep them in a cellar, give them food and water for several days and, if something does happen, then just issue directives to all those whom you know -- just say, 'Kill the extremists' -- on the spot, in the streets, anywhere, in the barracks compound, just shoot to kill in the stomach. It will not be a war, it will be a civil war in which there will be no mercy for anyone -- no mercy for women and no mercy shown to the children. Kill them in their flats, just simply a bomb in the family flat. At the decisive moment, yes, organise two or three men for the liquidation of those who are most dangerous, alright? Yes, the physical liquidation -- well, alright. Dum, dum, dum, and that will be that. Our police does not dare, but it agrees -- yes, it does dare, you go to one, and then you go to another and then you go to everybody at the same time. Those who are the most dangerous can be killed in front of their door steps. No questions asked. Don't worry whether they are women, children -- no questions asked."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: As early as 24 March 1990, at the Vukovar area, paramilitary formations were organised by Tomislav Mercep and Glavas which were later to grow in to the 204th Brigade of the National Guard Corps. On 10 March 1991, they organised a review of volunteers' detachments of paramilitary formations of Croatia which was attended by about 2,000 Croat people. Groups for silent liquidation in Vukovar and the surrounding villages were set up. (Videotape played).

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This is the mayor of Osijek. This is a display of paramilitary formations in Bogdanovci. "Commanders leaders, line up, one and all. Cipa, leave the papers alone! Everybody line up, please. Pero Maric, where is he? Yes, here he is. Maric, here he is, at the end. Maric has given over his papers. Yes, I have given them over to you. May I have a little silence, please? On order from the President of the Republic of Croatia, we must form -- a little silence, please -- more quiet -- be a little quieter. By order of the President of the Republic of Croatia, we formed unarmed detachments. You must know what we are talking about here. We have received orders to select the best men whom are going to serve in the Ministry of Internal Affairs. So, if you are on the list, then you will be part of these formations. On the next occasion, we are going to set up the medical corps, along with our detachments. We have 30 per cent of the possible people we need, which means that you will have to get to know the commanders, who are going to be located in Graza in Bogdanovci and then will explain to one and all who the commanders are and, please, see who the shady characters -- the suspect characters are. Just note them down if you think that anybody is shady or suspect. Nothing is a secret any more. There are no more secrets, so we are going to set up unarmed detachments and we are going to organise them. There is no need to keep a secret any longer, but if anybody is suspect, just make a note of their names, because we have been told that there are shady characters in our midst, so we will try and list them in that way. Let me tell you one thing: as far as weapons are concerned, we have the necessary weapons. We have them now, there are no more problems about that and we are going to have to start training, because I do not want people coming here untrained. You are going to learn what we are going to do, we have formed the detachments, we have formed the medical corps, we will form even larger detachments and we are going to have training -- we are going to do this in agreement with the Ministry of Internal Affairs. You are going to go to your own departments and make a list of the names -- those who do not belong on the list -- and we all know who these are -- just strike them off. We will make a note of this, and then I will tell them what the President told us. I am not going to speak about arms. I have explained the armament situation to you. We are going to form unarmed detachments for the following reasons, and we are going to line up and go and take a look at the headquarters in Bogdanovci and then up to Luzac and then the bunker in Luzac. This is the Serb part from here to Osijek. We are going to solve that situation and the other region will be settled by the others, so this whole territory has been covered. We must link up the road from Bogdanovci and Nustar. Is everybody going up there or just the commanders? No, everybody. Turn around, please. Line up; you must line up properly so we can see who is present and who is not. There's enough space. The headquarters for Vukovar, Osijek and Vinkovski. The commanders, would you please make some order here? Vjiselko, where is Vjiselko? The President of the Republic of Croatia, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, has given us the go-ahead to form unarmed detachments for the first time of the civilian defence of the Democratic Union, for the first time publicly and freely. At this meeting, we are going to make up a list of the most capable individuals and the most vital part of all of us and we are going to recommend to the Ministry of the Interior that we strengthen our ranks as an army formation. We have gathered you here today to organise unarmed detachments so that we can organise a medical corps later on and to inform you with the headquarters and your commanders for the area of Vukovar. We are going to have another relocated command position in the village of Babska, and the headquarters, the staff in Bogdanovci. Bogdanovci has been chosen because it is located on part of territory inhabited by Serbs, to Brsadina until Osijek whereas the other portion of the territory is inhabited by us, so we will be able to form a front there just so that you know the strategy. Bogdanovci has been covered with bunkers from Luzac to Nustar and you are now going to see our headquarters, so that if something happens to your commander or leader, each and every one of you will know -- will convey this information to the people that have not been able to come here today, so that they know where to take up their positions and we will have our links by courier. There are some radio devices which are unreliable, so communication must be held alive through courier. Anybody who sees that somebody is working against the Croat republic, make a note of his name and make a note of any counter intelligence going on. You must not trust anybody but listen to orders. The President of the Republic of Croatia has asked us that, as we have been patient up to now, to show wisdom and patience from now on, because every day is working in our favour. I know that it is difficult for you to come up here, but we must see what we have at our disposal, the men and equipment, and you know that everybody has come from the local communities and it represents a third of all available forces. We have not called any women here today, but next time we are going to call up some women to make up the medical corps and we will have more devices -- we have some devices now -- you are going to have to learn to handle them. And, if it is necessary, we must know how to handle these devices. So, we are all gathered here together, calmly, to hear how we are going to act and organise ourselves, and the people living in Bogdanovci know this area better than I do. Vinko, here he is, let's all form a column, four by four, towards the Graza area. Let us have a walk around the area so we become better acquainted with it. I should also like to ask you to dispel slowly and if you are asked by anybody what you were doing here, say you were preparing for the gymnastics display to celebrate Republic Day on 30 May."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At the beginning of May 1991 the intimidation culminated in this area. During the night on Wednesday 1 May, two Croat policemen appeared in a police car in Borovo Selo, this is a Serb village not far from Vukovar. One of them opened fire from an automatic weapon and the other tore up the Yugoslav flag. The provocations continued on the following day. Josip Daja, the chief of the Croat police, sent another 20 men of his to Borovo Selo. But his buses were greeted with salvos from automatic weapons fired by the villagers. Twelve Croat policemen and three Serb civilians died in this incident. The fuse of the inter-ethnic conflict had been lit. The sequel could be predicted. Croats, Mladen Miljkovic and Ivica Zrnic slit the throats of two soldiers on 15 August 1991. Before that, they were brutally tortured. Let us also mention that three days later they also committed a crime against a girl, Sladana Petrovic, whom they raped, tortured and brutally killed. The same persons took part in crimes in August 1991, against 15 men and five women in Olajnica. In another room, in which there were about 20 women with their children, on the orders of Ivica Zrnic, Mladen Mirkovic slit the throats of two boys of about 15 years who were tied to chairs. They liquidated a group of 10 people. The bodies were thrown down somewhere in the direction of Borovo. More and more criminals appeared and the number of victims multiplied. For example, Ivan Kapular usually threw his victims into the Danube. He was on the active force of the ZNG, the commander of the Defence of Borovo Nasilje, a member of the command of the Vukovar Brigade. In his headquarters at the Abazija pizza parlour in Borovo Naselje, in a cellar, he would interrogate, with a group of his people, persons who had been brought in, tortured them and killed them, and then threw them into the Danube. The following were killed on his orders: Tihomir Kovacevic, Predrag Ciric, Svetozar Vladisavljevic, Simo Sirota, Milorad Tesic, Dara Grujic, Milana Siladi and Nikola Cancarevic. The same was done by Zoran Sipos who led a group with Martin Sabljic and Nikola Cibaric. From the Nova Obuca shelter they hauled out the elderly married couple Dragoljub and Milica Vracaric, stole 42,000 Dinars from them and shot them. Nothing is known about the group of Serbs who took shelter in the Dom Tehnike on 28 October 1991 - Zoran Petrovic, Mladen Jovic, Radovan Lukicevic, Jovica Leskovac, Vojo Dekic, Ranko Perkovic, and Mileta Stankovic. Zoran Sipos and his cronies effaced all traces of their existence. The Defence is presenting supporting material in connection with all of this, and these are binding sentences of the military court in Belgrade. You can see this and I submitted this to you and to the Prosecution and the Registry. I kindly request that we show another video clip, from which you will see what happened at the JNA barracks and in Bjelovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Can I ask you to explain the origin of these videotapes -- who shot the tapes -- this applies also to the last one?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: It was filmed by the Croats but they forgot that the Yugoslav television displayed it, too. I received it from the Yugoslav television and also the next videotapes you will see, so they are undeniable. Now you also see a mark logo of the television, too. (Videotape played). Strangling of a soldier, Split, 6 May 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This soldier was a Macedonian. (Videotape continued).

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Bjelovar, September 1991, massacre of members of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: 40 groups were identified and hundreds of criminals on the territory of Vukovar. The military court in Belgrade identified over 100 members of the ZNG and the Ministry of the Interior of Croatia. A small number was brought to justice and convicted. At that time, the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA, comprised soldiers of all nationalities from the territory of the SFRY suffered special forms of pressure starting in 1991. During the summer and autumn of that year, Croat paramilitary forces attacked JNA units. First they would surround the barracks, carry out various acts of sabotage and finally kill soldiers regardless of their nationality. The JNA barracks in Delnice, Koprivnica, Virovitica, Osijek and Bjelovar were surrounded in this way. These were cities in which armed conflicts had not broken out. The JNA barracks in Vukovar was under blockade for several weeks. All communications were severed, the soldiers remained without food and water, in a word, without they were without the basic necessities of life. All the efforts of the JNA and the political bodies of the former SFRY to solve that problem in a peaceful way were of no avail. The situation constantly worsened. Many soldiers lost their lives in their barracks compounds. I now kindly request you view two video clips, the one from Split which we already have seen, and the one from Bjelovar. The barracks in Bjelovar where the ZNG members killed several members of the JNA -- you will see that now. (Videotape played). The JNA barracks in Bjelovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That is barracks without any Serbs -- on the territory of Croatia. These are not Serbs, Sir. (Videotape continued). This is the Croat State and it is going to be free of occupiers and Chetniks. We are going to liberate it. Until the very last, it will never fall. For the home and freedom, but only to the Croat people. This is a young man, he is active -- well, he is not really active. He is a reservist, possibly. There were very few active soldiers. Our army has to be a lasting foundation of our independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The conflicts in Vukovar started and the fighting lasted for several months. The city suffered severe damage. The Vukovar hospital, by definition a protected building under the relevant conventions, was used for precisely opposite purposes. The Croat paramilitary carried out combat operations from that building, which Dr. Skow has also testified to before this court, as Dr. Ivankovic in his statement which I am presenting as supporting material. Why did the Serb people take up arms to defend themselves in the Vukovar area? Apart from their collective memory of their suffering in 1941, the Serbs were apprehensive of the secession of the Republic of Croatia -- and they had good grounds for that -- from the SFRY and for good reason, for they had already seen a constitution turning them from a constituent nation into a national minority promulgated. Everything which happened later only justified their fears. Of course, the Serb people organised themselves for the defence and formed in the areas in which they lived the Republic of Srpska Krajina covering a third of the territory of Croatia. They were, once again in their history, trying to prevent the crime of which they had been the greatest victim during the Second World War. I kindly request that we show video clip 6 on the suffering of Serbs in Vukovar. (Videotape played) "This is the JNA entering Vukovar. The one lying there on his stomach, that is Ilija Vukovic. This is his home, the house that has been torn down, the one here, the one lying here on his stomach -- no, rather on his back -- that is his house, a Serb, too. This woman lying here, over the old lady, the first one here, that is the wife of Ilija Vukovic and I do not know these two women. I cannot see their faces. I know about the three of them, though."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The result of the attempt of the Serbs to win the right of their own State is today clear to everyone. In 1995, the Croat army mounted the famous "Flash" and "Storm" operations and, in a short while, expelled the Serb population from the regions of Northern Dalmatia, Lika, Banja, Kordun and Western Slavonia. Of course, those who survived. The Serbs were banished from their ancestral homes. Croatia successfully gained an ethnically pure Croat population within its present State borders. The Serbs in the area of Eastern Slavonia suffered the same fate, this time not through a military operation but at the negotiating table. According to the Erdut Agreement, it was given to the Republic of Croatia. What does this look like numerically? The answer can be found in the publication "1991 Population Census -- the Ethnic Composition of Croatia Settlement by Settlement". (Republican Institute of Statistics of the Republic of Croatia, Zagreb, April 1991. Preface, Dr. Jakov Gelo, Director of the Institute). A quote: " Croatia is the state of the Croats. The Serbs are the most numerous national minority in Croatia. At the time of the 1991 census they numbered 581,663 people. The Serbs were an absolute or relative majority in 1,105 Croat settlements." . According to statements made in the publication, the total number of inhabitants of the Republic of Croatia in 1991 was 4,784,265, which means that Serbs accounted for over 12 per cent. The same publication gives the total number of settlements in the Republic of Croatia from which it follows that Serbs constituted an absolute or relative majority in over 17 per cent of the total number of settlements. After the "Flash" and "Storm" operations and the Erdut agreement, 127,000 Serbs remained in Croatia. Today, there are only 67,000 of them. Hence, from 1991 to the end of 1997, the Republic of Croatia managed to reduce the number of its inhabitants as per the 1991 Census by over half a million Serbs. This time, all the doors have closed. The idea of Ante Starcevic, through the genocidal crimes of Ante Pavelic, to the ethnically pure Croatia of Franjo Tudjman, has finally come full circle. From 1941 and the time of the independent State of Croatia, through the "brotherhood and unity" of the SFRY, to the present when that State no longer exists, over 90 per cent of the Serbs in Croatia have been driven into exile or physically destroyed. The number of Serbs living in Croatia today is only symbolic. According to the latest estimates at the beginning of this year, that number decreased by a further 30,000 to 35,000 so that if the mentioned Dr. Galo were to a write a population census in the year 2001, he could, in his introduction, repeat the same slogan, "Croatia is the State of the Croats" and he would be 100 per cent. Today Europe can envy Croatia, it is ethnically the most homogenous State of the old continent. With the permission of your Honours, I am going to go faster through the next portion, because it deals with the United Nations. From 9 November until this year --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, may I ask you whether you could kindly summarise this section on the impotence of the international community to protect the Serbs, or even skip it? Please, slow down!

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That is exactly what I asked for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Do not speak too fast, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: As regards point B, there are 15 resolutions of the Security Council of the United Nations that were submitted. They all deal with one common idea and that is that the Security Council of the United Nations calls upon the Government of the Republic of Croatia to honour its commitments and the last one is from 6 May this year. In the meantime, Serb cemeteries in Vukovar were devastated. Over 2,000 Serbs went to Norway and the number of Serbs has been reduced to a very large extent. What is not clear is how many more resolutions of the Security Council of this kind will be passed. Probably not too many, because, when the last Serb has left, there will be no reason to pass such security resolutions by the Security Council of the United Nations. Now I am going to move on to the resolutions, or, rather, I wish to say in the supporting material you have the relevant resolutions and now I wish to move on to point C, Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic, his curriculum vitae so that we know who we are dealing with. The family of Slavko Dokmanovic has been living in the area of the municipality of Trpinja for over 250 years. He was born in 1949 and lived and worked in that area until he was forced to leave it and flee to Sombor as a refugee. He graduated from the Faculty of Agriculture in Osijek in 1974 and after serving in the army got a job with the VUPIK company. Since May 1990, at the first multi-Party elections, as an SDP (Party of Democratic Changes) candidate, which won the elections, he was appointed to the office of the chairman of the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar. He held this post until the beginning of June 1991, when he was told to leave the post. He lived in the house 10 kilometres from Vukovar, until he was expelled, and commuted to work every day. Croat patrols stopped him on the road as he went to work and carried out checks and searches for no reason. So after that, on 23 July 1991, he was formally relieved of his duties. That same day, the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar was dissolved according to a decision of the Government of the Republic of Croatia. He continued to live in his village and the office of chairman of the Municipal Assembly was held by the then deputy chairman Marin Vidic Bili. On 23 July 1991, he was formally installed as representative of the Government of the Republic of Croatia in the City of Vukovar, which is four months before these events. Slavko Dokmanovic was not a President or anything else at the time. His political engagement began in August 1991. He was appointed Minister of Agriculture, because he graduated from the Faculty of Agriculture for the District of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem. He performed tasks relating to the development of agriculture, the protection, use, and improvement of agricultural land, forests and water, flora and fauna, the development of the countryside, the food industry, the water industry, and water supply, and other tasks. I have supplied you with the law and the ministries of the Serb District of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem, article 10 of the official gazette of the Serb District No. 1. You can see a description of these activities. At the end of 1991, when the Serb Krajina was established and its Government formed Slavko Dokmanovic held no Government office in the Republic of Serbia Krajina at all. He worked at the Vinarija in Vukovar until 1994. The Municipal Assembly of Vukovar was constituted in 1993. Slavko Dokmanovic was elected chairman of the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar, once again in 1994. He held that post until 5 April 1996, when he was relieved of office. He continued to live in Trpinja and, as a refugee, went to Sombor. He lived in Sombor with his family, where his family lives today and he lived there until his arrest and until he was brought to The Hague. Slavko Dokmanovic was brought before the County Court in Osijek, accused of criminal offences other than the ones he is charged with before this Tribunal and he had to leave Croatia. I should like to underline the following paradox: if proof really existed for the acts he is charged with in the indictment, he would probably have answered for the same acts before the County Court in Osijek, but he was never brought up on charges like the ones brought against him here. The political functions of Slavko Dokmanovic: At the time covered by the indictment, he neither formally nor actually held the office of chairman of the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar. The Defence will present evidence to the effect that, from June 1991, he was prevented from holding that office. The assembly was dissolved and stopped working on 23 July 1991. That marks the formal end of the term of office of Slavko Dokmanovic. From that time onwards Marin Vidic Bili held the post of representative of the Government of Croatia. Dokmanovic was again elected chairman of the newly formed assembly only in 1994. The documents and opinions of experts will prove that it was practically impossible to gain such a post for Dokmanovic under the circumstances prevailing until the end of 1991 and that it is legal fiction in charges and that this was impossible under the circumstances that prevailed in those areas at the end of 1991, and, as I say, that it is a legal fiction in the charges. Vukovar was under military rule in the period to which the indictment refers. It was a period immediately following the end of the fighting, or where fighting was still going on. According to the testimony of the witnesses, Vesna Bosanac and Marin Vidic and others all negotiation were conducted with JNA officers because there was no civilian authority in Vukovar and therefore no President of the municipality of Vukovar. The first civilian authority of Vukovar was formed pursuant to a decision of the Government of the Serb district of Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem on 28 November 1991 at the end of the war operations. At that time, Srbobran Bibic was elected President of the Executive Council of the municipality of Vukovar. This council actually started working only in mid December 1991, as it gradually took over from the military authorities' various levels of responsibility for normal life in the city. The Executive Council performed its functions until it was discharged in 1993, which is when the assembly of the municipality of Vukovar was set up and its first President was Vojislav Stanimirovic, who is the leader of the Serbs at the present time in that region. Slavko Dokmanovic was elected chairman of the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar in 1994 for the second time. It is important to note that, while holding that post for the first time in 1991, he undertook activities aimed at the peaceful resolution of the crisis - that is why he was not popular either with the extremist Serbs or the extremist Croats. From the abundance of available material, we shall present his speeches, newspaper articles and videotapes attesting to his unreserved commitment to the peaceful resolution of the conflict. May I have tape number 7 now, please, which is one of the segments that I wish to show you? (Videotape played). "Today's information of the Serb Montenegrin Party of the President of Yugoslavia that tomorrow I cannot be present at the peace conference in Yugoslavia and The Hague --"

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: This is an error, sorry, just a moment. I apologise, your Honours, there has been an error, which we shall put right in just a moment. Your Honours, I would take advantage of this opportunity to ask you and the Prosecutors, when I come to the end of point 7, Slavko Dokmanovic's alibi, and points B and analysis of the witnesses, I will move over this quicker, because I will be giving this analysis later on, and you have the text anyway. You have it before you, so I will skip over this part of the analysis of the statements of the Prosecution witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Is it fine with you if we take a break in 10 minutes, or you can tell me when you think it is appropriate -- 10 minutes -- because the interpreters --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, let us say 10 minutes. We shall be over in about 10 minutes. (Videotape played) "Because of the disturbing situation in the villages of the Vukovar municipality with the predominantly Serb population, the President of the Municipal Assembly, Slavko Dokmanovic, invited all the citizens to show level-headedness and to wait for the unfolding of the crisis calmly."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In the second mandate, once again, he advocated the peaceful integration of this area into the Republic of Croatia and the result was his participation in the agreements which later led to the Erdut agreement. You have numerous photographs in the supporting evidence, which bears this out, both with Mr. Klein, Mr. Rowan, and others. In that period, no-one applied to him for permission to carry out exhumations at Ovcara, as such permission was to be obtained only from the Government of the Republic of Serb Krajina or the UNTAES, which we already had occasion to hear about in the testimonies of the Prosecution's witnesses. As the Defence has mentioned, Slavko Dokmanovic held the office of chairman of the Municipal Assembly of Vukovar twice, but he certainly did not hold that office at the time of the events at Ovcara. C: The alibi of Slavko Dokmanovic for 19, 20 and 21 November -- you have received this in written form by the Defence on several occasions -- the 19th and 20th has already been claimed by the Prosecution. As far as 20 November is concerned, we are going to show, by a videotape and the witnesses to be seen on the videotape, that Slavko Dokmanovic, on 20 November 1991, could not have been at Ovcara, because, at around 8 a.m., he left his home with witnesses Jovo Cvetkovic and Rade Leskovac for Backa Palanka. At 9 a.m., he arrived at Backa Palanka where he spent some time with Ljuba Novakovic, the President of the Municipal Assembly in the building with members of delegations from Kladovo, et cetera. Some time after 12 noon, he set out with Jova Cvetkovic, Nebojsa Lazarevic, Zoran Jeftovic and Rade Leskovac towards Vukovar and the evacuation of the victims from the hospital had already taken place, and they were in front of the barracks in Vukovar. After 3.30 p.m., he arrived in Vukovar, and he entered a VELEPROMET enterprise a little before 2 o'clock -- he arrived at 1.30 p.m. At that time the buses with the victims left the barracks and were in the Ovcara hangar. There was a Government meeting in the VELEPROMET enterprise, and Dokmanovic was in the company of numerous Ministers and witnesses at that Government meeting. At 3.30 p.m. he left the VELEPROMET enterprise, and, with his fellow travellers, went to the centre of Vukovar, where he granted the witness Vukosav Tomasevic an interview for Radio Polimlje. Polimlje is a settlement in southern Serbia. Some time before 4 p.m. Slavko Dokmanovic left the city in a motorcade heading out of Vukovar. Before 5 p.m., an incident occurred at the checkpoint barrier at Oriolik, which means that they had left Vukovar a long time ago, when Slavko Dokmanovic came into conflict with members of the military police barring passage to his vehicle. At 5.30 p.m. he arrived in Sidski Banovci, which is a town on Serb territory. At 6.30 p.m. he left with Rade Leskovac to his home in Trpinja via Ilok and Erdut. He arrived home at about 8 p.m. There is no doubt that he was on the territory afterwards and the Prosecution agrees with me and this is the case for the 21st as well. Thank you. In the written portion, the Defence provides an analysis of the statements of the Prosecution witnesses. I am going to pass over this section quickly, because you have it before you in writing, and I will mention it again in my summing up. Two witnesses confirmed that they personally saw Slavko Dokmanovic for a short while two to five minutes in the hangar at the Ovcara farm in the interval between 2 and 4 p.m. The other witnesses did not see Slavko Dokmanovic or even claim that he was in any of the four relevant places at which the indictment sees him. These sites are the hospital, the barracks, the hangar, and the execution site. These two witnesses did not see him at those three points, whereas the indictment sees him there. The Defence considers that these two witnesses are not to be believed. This Tribunal has examples where the witnesses of the Prosecution's Office have been shown to be unreliable. In the first case, the first possibility is that these witnesses are not telling the truth, either on their own initiative, or on orders from somebody else. This happened with Witness L in the case of the accused Dusko Tadic, who said, before this Tribunal, that he was ordered to give testimony against Tadic. The second possibility, which is a much more probable one, is that the witness was wrong, given the specific mental state he was in, and that he simply confused persons in his memory. This same case happened before this same Tribunal with the witness Nesiha Klipic in the Grabez case before this Tribunal, but the case was held before the military court in Switzerland when the witness claimed she had watched Grabez on a tank for 30 minutes. However, the court established that he had been in Germany at the time in question, thus the court accepted the alibi and explained that the witness Klipic was deluded and did not lend credence to her statement. In short, the witness had mixed up the individuals she was identifying. This second variation is more probable than the first. The Defence presented a table of the witnesses Berghofer and Cakalic. The differences in their testimonies to the Defence and to this Tribunal and the differences that occur in the statements and their newspaper interviews -- we provide a table of the differences, because they do not coincide and agree on any points apart from the fact that Slavko Dokmanovic was there. They do not agree as to time, place, or anything else. They talk about a blue pilot's uniform which nobody has ever seen -- airman's uniform -- and the Prosecutor said that he was wearing a camouflage uniform anyway. Then we have mention of a blue pilot's uniform, and the other one testifies to a blue JNA uniform with the rank of colonel. One of them saw a five-pointed star on the head of the Tito cap; one speaks of a blue pilot's uniform with a sweat suit top to protect him from the rain -- a dark blue in colour -- and he sees a jacket, a shirt and tie, whereas the other individual saw a Tito cap with a five-pointed star on the head and no sweat suit top. Berghofer saw a pilot's uniform -- I do not know what the aviation would have been doing there anyway. As to rank, Berghofer did not see the rank of lieutenant colonel whereas the Cakalic statement did see the rank of lieutenant colonel. Berghofer said there was no Chetnik, whereas the Prosecution says this was a key individual and was there for two to five minutes -- 10 minutes -- and said that this was a key individual. What key individual could have been there for such a short time? Berghofer thought that Dokmanovic was commanding the hangar. Then he later says that he did not have this impression. In his statement he does not say he was kicked with the leg. I have provided you with a complete table, so that you can see what and who -- who, what, when was stated. I can read out something else. There is a third possibility as well -- apart from the cases of Tadic and Grabez, the witnesses did see Dokmanovic sooner or later who they knew earlier on. Berghofer knew him better. Berghofer can easily be mistaken because he did not know him well and Cakalic because his glasses were broken and he had blood in his eyes. Both, in their own words, were beaten up and in terrible fear of their lives. There were many people at Ovcara and some of them resembled Dokmanovic. Mention is made of an officer with a moustache -- Dokmanovic has a moustache. Some people of his own age, his own height and his build, some majors and lieutenant colonels were mentioned as well, so it is possible to make a mistake, and that it was a mistake. The best proof of that is the blue uniform of an air force lieutenant colonel of the JNA, which they only saw, and such a uniform as they describe does not exist in the JNA. Different type of uniforms were described -- camouflage, Territorial Defence uniforms and JNA uniforms, but nobody saw a blue uniform, especially not one worn by an air force lieutenant colonel. The Defence emphasises something else as well. I have sent you a copy of the interview of Berghofer and it is interesting that witnesses have the need to explain their behaviour to the newspaper. So, Berghofer, in his interview, states: "We have put Dokmanovic behind bars. We shall be doing the same with Mrksic." This was to be found in the "Arena" magazine of 1998. Who "we" are and who has been put behind bars is not quite clear. Finally -- I will be over in two minutes -- the most important question is how we can, on the basis of statements of this kind, bear out the Prosecutor's point stated in the pre-trial materials, and the fact that the Defence will bring several witnesses, which will bear out the key role played by Dokmanovic, and his direct or indirect involvement in the crime that we are dealing with -- does this evidence bear that out, that he had knowledge on the location that he had bulldozers for excavating the grave, organised buses, found executioners, misled the international observers and so on and so forth -- all this, in a matter of two to five minutes when he appeared at Ovcara, as the witnesses say. The second witness said that the bulldozer was there all the time and that he had selected the site and that it was some unknown officer and not Dokmanovic, whom he actually knew. On 20 November he was in a hunting suit which can be seen on the tape. It is no camouflage uniform. It is a hunting suit, because there was no water and no food, et cetera. He wore that same suit for two to three months. You will see on several occasions in several interviews, he was dressed the same way. It was not a blue pilot's uniform worn by a lieutenant colonel as the witnesses say. From the written evidence, we can see that he was neither an officer nor a soldier of the JNA, nor in any paramilitary formation. Therefore, he could neither have commanded nor carried out any supervision or command, as claimed in counts 25 and 26 of the indictment. He neither knew nor saw the accused officers Mrksic, Sljivancanin and Radic, nor any participants in the events in the hangar at Ovcara. In any case, had Dokmanovic been at Ovcara, according to the testimony of the Prosecution Witness Q, he himself would have been liquidated, because they resented his having saved the remaining Croat policemen in Borovo Selo from liquidation and for not having armed the Serbs in Ovcara. You will hear more about this tomorrow. The Defence will prove using a video tape and the testimonies of witnesses on that tape as well as other witnesses and exhibits in evidence, that Dokmanovic was not at the Ovchara farm even for even those two minutes at the time asserted in the indictment either intentionally or by chance, as the witness states. The Defence will prove that Slavko Dokmanovic not only did not play a key role, as the Prosecution wishes to prove, but did not have any part in these events. Simply the wrong man has been accused and arrested. We should ask ourselves whether Slavko Dokmanovic is being held to account instead of the real culprits, who are at present not before this Tribunal. We must have a little patience and, sooner or later, they will be brought to face international justice. I think this is a good time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. We stand adjourned for 20 minutes. (10.05 a.m.). (A short break). (10.30 a.m.).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Legal issues. The indictment charges Slavko Dokmanovic on six counts. He is charged with grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions, violations of the laws or customs of war and crimes against humanity (counts 1, 2 and 3 refer to the beating that happened at Ovcara and counts 4, 5 and 6 refer to the killings which occurred in connection with the large scale crime which took place there). None of these counts is alternative, but they are cumulative to the best of the Defence's understanding. Grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions according to the Geneva Conventions, the nature of the conflict in the territory of the former Yugoslavia -- the Prosecutor claims that it was an international armed conflict and it is incorrect and unfounded. The Geneva Conventions from 1949 cannot be applied, so counts 1 and 4 have to be rejected. It seems that the Prosecutor treats the declaration of independence of 25 June 1991 of Croatia as an undeniable legal act. This is not based either on international or internal law. Croatia seceded from Yugoslavia and obtained independence in a process of rebellion, which, according to our internal law, was a criminal offence, and, in this way, it was in contravention of the rules of international law. The qualification of the declaration of independence as a legally permissible act can cause disastrous effects in terms of international stability and international order. This can be understood as support to all secessionist movements in the world and I believe this was not the intention of the Prosecutor. The Prosecutor's claim that "Croatia was clearly considered to be independent from 8 October 1991" (pre-trial brief page 12) is actually a very dubious one. In addition to that, it is not of particular legal importance. In spite of the proclamation of independence on 25 June 1991 until the end of 1991, Croatia took part in the Federal authorities of the SFRY. On 27 November 1991, in Geneva, the representatives of the SFRY, the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Serbia signed a Memorandum of Understanding, where it was made possible to apply the Geneva Conventions from 1949, or some of their rules for the protection of individuals and for hostilities. With the permission of your Honours, I am going to say exhibit 1, 2, 3, 4, because this is supporting materials, so that you can be following what I am saying so that you could check whether what I am saying is true, or not. So I am talking about exhibit 1. The signing of the memorandum would have been pointless on 29 November 1991 -- was Croatia considered to be an independent State, a contracting State according to the Geneva Conventions from 8 October 1991? Some people think the signing of the memorandum had an effect on the international nature of the conflict. This is quite wrong. There is no proof to support this. The general provisions of the memorandum include the following: the application of the previous provisions will not affect the legal status and the memorandum follows The Hague declaration of 5 November 1991, where the observance of International humanitarian Law should be ensured and this was signed by the Presidents of the six Republics. It would be illogical, legally, that the parties to the agreement sign an agreement to carry out Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions. They have to abide by the Geneva Conventions and Article 3 by virtue of the Geneva Conventions themselves, had they been independent, of course. The agreement in the field of international humanitarian law has a point only if they are prepared to observe this and this was the case here. Even this Croatia considered to be independent at that time on 8 October 1991. If it was an independent State then and if it thought that it had obtained independence then and if, that is, had they believe post factum, this is legally unimportant. It is only facts that are of a decisive importance from then, from a legal point of view -- not what happened if in 1992 and 1993 as the Prosecution says and then to recognise that retroactively. We are dealing in this trial with what happened in 1991 and Croatia did not exist as an independent State and from that date it is said that Croatia obtained all the criteria for obtaining independence and this is again from the Prosecutor's brief and this is not based on facts or law. Two simultaneous processes of rebellion were taking place at that time in the Croatia and SFRY. One of the processes was the armed rebellion of the Croats against the JNA -- the Croat forces against the JNA whose units were legally present on the territory of Croatia, because it was then part of the territory of the SFRY. The second parallel process is the armed rebellion of the Serbs against the new Croat Government. In this situation, the new Croat Government did not hold under its control a large part of Croat territory and they were in conflict with the local Serbs and the JNA. In addition to that, the relevant situation was characterised by a massive violation of the rights of Serbs in Croatia during the relevant period of time. (INAUDIBLE) confidence and peace in Yugoslavia, organised by the international community, was active in seeking a peaceful solution. Finally, the recognition of the Republic of Croatia was carried out on 15 January 1992 by the members of the European Community, and that was assessed by important politicians as having been premature. The way in which the Prosecutor approaches the so-called Badinter Commission (page 13 of the brief) to prove its legal position, does not meet the high expectations of the legal community of the world in this respect. The Prosecutor invokes only one paragraph of the rich legal opus of the Badinter Commission and this is an incomplete quote. It is more than surprising that the Prosecutor did not cite the most relevant statement of the Badinter Commission expounded in opinion number 1 of 29 November 1991, which reads as follows: "Although so far the SFRY has retained its international personality, notably inside international organisations, the Republics have expressed their desire for independence." This is in the future. B: "In Croatia a referendum held in May 1991 followed by a declaration of independence on 25 June 1991, which was suspended for three months, and confirmed on 8 October 1991." The recourse of force has led to armed conflict between the different elements of the federation which has caused the death of thousands of people and wrought considerable destruction within a few months only. The authorities of the federation and the republics have shown themselves to be powerless to enforce respect for the succeeding cease-fire agreements concluded under the auspices of the European communities or the United Nations organisation (exhibit number 2 which I have presented). It is quite clear that the Badinter Commission qualified then (namely, on 29 November 1991) the conflict as an internal conflict. The arbitration commission qualified the conflict, and I underline this, as "an armed conflict between different elements of the federation". Then, on 29 November 1991, the Badinter Commission treated "declaration of independence on 25 June 1991", which was suspended for three months, only that the republic had expressed interests its desire for independence. At that time, the Badinter Commission did not find that Croatia had acquired its independence. Furthermore, the Prosecutor failed to quote the relevant statements of the Badinter Commission contained in its opinion number 5 of 11 January 1992 on the recognition of the Republic of Croatia by the European Community and its member States, when the Commission considered the constitutional act of 4 December 1991 does not fully incorporate all the provisions of the draft convention of 4 November 1991, notably those contained in Chapter 2, Article 2(c) under the heading "Special Status". The authorities of the Republic of Croatia should therefore supplement the constitutional act in such a way as to satisfy those provisions and, subject to this reservation, the Republic of Croatia meets the necessary conditions for its recognition by the Member States of the European Community in accordance with the declaration on Yugoslavia and the guidelines on the recognition of new States in Eastern Europe and in the Soviet Union adopted by the Council of the European Communities on 16 December 1991. This is exhibit number 3. If the Badinter Commission was of the opinion on 11 January 1992 that Croatia, even at a normative constitutional level, did not meet the legitimate expectation concerning the protection of the Serb minority, who could expect that the SFRY, before that date, saw Croatia as an independent State, namely, a State which is prepared to respect its international obligations, including those concerning protection of minorities? The full text of the paragraph 11 of 16 July 1993 quoted by the Prosecutor, in part, reads as follows, and I shall read the entire text now: "The issue is the same as regards the Republics of Croatia and Slovenia, both of which declared their independence on 25 June 1991, and suspended their declaration of independence for three months on 7 July 1991 as provided by the Brijuni Declaration." In accordance with the declaration the suspension ceased to have effect on 8 October 1991 -- only then did those two Republics definitely break all links with the organs of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and become sovereign States in international law. For them then 8 October 1991 is the date of State succession (exhibit number 4). The underlined part of the sentence is not in the quotation -- yes, break all links with organs of the SFRY is of importance for the consideration of the date of acquisition of independence by the two republics, but it is not correct that the Republic of Croatia, on 8 October 1991, did break all links with the organs of the SFRY. That is why the Prosecutor did not quote that. Simply this is not true. We shall demonstrate that it is wrong -- if the premise is not correct, the conclusion cannot be correct, either. Finally, opinions of the Badinter Commission are without legal force and they are not legally binding. I shall kindly ask to show the last part of the videotape. You are now going to see Mr. Mesic. On 6 November (INAUDIBLE) Stjepan Mesic, President of the Presidency of the SFRY appeared at the 8th plenary session of the Conference for Peace in Yugoslavia held in The Hague (exhibit number 10). That is exhibit number 16. The International Law Commission is therefore of the opinion that a determination of aggression comes under the exclusive competence of the UN Security Council. It is therefore clear that determining acts of aggression, breaches or threats of peace is reserved for the Security Council. It is therefore obvious that determining the nature of an armed conflict is an indivisible part of this exclusive competence of the Security Council itself. There is no reason for me to believe that the Security Council would wish to share this competence with anyone else, including this august Tribunal. Therefore, I conclude at the relevant time of this indictment, Croat forces were in conflict with local Serb forces and JNA forces. The Croat Government did not have any control over large parts of Croat territory. The Croat Government was not prepared to respect crucial laws of international law concerning human rights and the protection of minorities. Serb people in Croatia were exposed to crimes, including mass crimes performed by the Croat authorities. The Croat Government did not break its links with the organs of the SFRY. The conference for peace in Yugoslavia continued throughout this time. The Security Council treated the armed conflict in all its relevant resolutions as an internal conflict, and therefore the armed conflict, at the relevant time, was an internal conflict and is therefore not applicable and subject to the Geneva Conventions. E3, the Application of International Conventions in Armed Conflict: the concept of grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions for the protection of victims of war can be applied only in an international armed conflict, and this was an internal armed conflict on the territory of Croatia, that is to say, the territory of Vukovar. If the Prosecution persists in its position, there will be unforeseeable harmful consequences for the future application of international humanitarian law. It is inadmissible for the Prosecution not to acknowledge the sovereign will of States expressed at the conclusion or ratification or any other commitments undertaken by States to extend on the basis of Article 3 mini conventions, the application of the Geneva Conventions for the protection of the victims of war from 1949, also in an armed conflict. That is present in many of the indictments by the Prosecution. The Prosecutor is endeavouring to prove the existence of an international armed conflict on the territory of the former SFRY, because he is so compelled by the unfounded position of the Appeals Chamber in the Tadic case. The position of the Appeals Chamber totally disregards in this specific instance in the former SFRY, the obviously expressed will of the parties to the conflict to respect the rules of international law. Such a position totally rules out the possibility and sends a clear message to future parties to internal armed conflicts that they can freely conclude agreements on the basis of Article 3 common to the Geneva Conventions for the protection of victims of war, but they can freely violate them because they will not be punished. Therefore, such a position is indubitably contrary to the very spirit and evolution of international humanitarian law and the trend to protect the widest possible circle of individuals and scope for the application of the rules in particular cases of armed conflicts. That is why we consider that it is understandable, the view of experts dealing with international humanitarian law, that it would be tragic for the future application of rules of international humanitarian law if that position were to become law and this is quite understandable. For the sake of truth, we would like to remind you that the victims at Ovcara also included persons who were foreign mercenaries, who, according to the rules of international law, do not fall within the category of protected persons. You have a German and a Frenchman, Jean-Pierre, or whatever his name is. In conclusion, the concept of the breaches of the 1949 Geneva Conventions may only be applied to an international armed conflict which is not the case in the Dokmanovic case for at the relevant time on the territory of Croatia there was no international armed conflict. The Geneva Conventions for the protection of victims of war of 1949 cannot be applied in this particular case, hence the Defence does not accept paragraphs 22 and 23 of the amended indictment. All persons in the relevant time enjoyed the protection only according to the provisions of Article 3 common to the Geneva Conventions, which refers to the protection of victims in an internal armed conflict and provides minimum standards of humane behaviour applicable to any armed conflict, irrespective of its nature. The provisions of Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions is well known to you all. Let me now go to an analysis -- move on to F, point F, analysis of Article 2(a), 2(c), Article 3, Article 5(a) and 5(i). Articles 2(a) and 2(c) of the Statute do not apply --
